To find the largest integer \( N \) less than 2010 that satisfies the conditions \( N \equiv 5 \pmod{7} \), \( N \equiv 10 \pmod{11} \), and \( N \equiv 10 \pmod{13} \), we start by combining the congruences for 11 and 13. Since \( N \equiv 10 \pmod{11} \) and \( N \equiv 10 \pmod{13} \), we have \( N - 10 \) divisible by \( \text{lcm}(11, 13) = 143 \). Thus, \( N = 143k + 10 \) for some integer \( k \).

Next, substitute \( N = 143k + 10 \) into \( N \equiv 5 \pmod{7} \):
\[
143k + 10 \equiv 5 \pmod{7}
\]
Since \( 143 \equiv 3 \pmod{7} \), this simplifies to:
\[
3k + 10 \equiv 5 \pmod{7} \implies 3k \equiv -5 \pmod{7} \implies 3k \equiv 2 \pmod{7}
\]
The modular inverse of 3 modulo 7 is 5 (since \( 3 \times 5 \equiv 1 \pmod{7} \)). Multiplying both sides by 5 gives:
\[
k \equiv 10 \pmod{7} \implies k \equiv 3 \pmod{7}
\]
Thus, \( k = 7m + 3 \) for some integer \( m \). Substituting back, we get:
\[
N = 143(7m + 3) + 10 = 1001m + 439
\]
We need \( N < 2010 \):
\[
1001m + 439 < 2010 \implies 1001m < 1571 \implies m < \frac{1571}{1001} \approx 1.568
\]
The largest integer \( m \) is 1. Substituting \( m = 1 \):
\[
N = 1001 \times 1 + 439 = 1440
\]
Verification shows \( 1440 \) satisfies all conditions. The next solution \( m = 2 \) gives \( N = 2441 \), which exceeds 2010.
